solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Concerned with getting eaten by being whole (8)

indicatorNotes.getting eaten by: whatever is eaten ends up inside the eater, so the first piece goes inside the second

blocks.note: an entity is a being, a thing that exists
re = concerning, with regard to

annotation.surface: Someone preoccupied with being swallowed up whole.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Being whole' looks like one phrase, as in being swallowed whole, but the last word stands alone as the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'the whole' of something and 'the entirety' of it are interchangeable nouns.

entries.clue: Promised another way of writing Old English? (7)

indicatorNotes.another way of writing: the same two words are to be set down differently, here with their order swapped

blocks.note: Eng = English, the standard abbreviation
aged = old

annotation.surface: A question about how to spell Anglo-Saxon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old English' looks like the name of a language; read it as two separate words and write them the other way round.
annotation.definitionFit: Promised in the sense of betrothed: a couple who have promised to marry are engaged.

entries.clue: Add up to two, with nothing subtracted (3)

indicatorNotes.subtracted: in arithmetic, what is subtracted is taken away, so the named letters leave TWO

blocks.note: used as it stands
TWO loses W (with) and O (nothing)

annotation.surface: An arithmetic instruction: sum to two, taking away zero.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With nothing subtracted' reads as 'minus zero', which changes nothing; in fact both words are letters to remove: W = with and O = nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: A British idiom: to tot up a bill is to add up its figures, and the phrasal verb splits so 'up' travels with the definition.

entries.clue: Alarm, say, about upright pole for head of circus tent (10)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so the alarm word surrounds the pole

blocks.note: an alarm is one example of a ringer, something that rings
a mast is an upright pole

annotation.surface: Rigging a big top: an alarm fixed round the tent pole.
annotation.walkthrough: The tent pole really belongs in a circus, so the surface hides its piece of wordplay in plain sight.
annotation.definitionFit: A description rather than a synonym: the ringmaster is the master of ceremonies who runs the show under the big top.

entries.clue: Electric weapon’s problem with energy escaping (5)

indicatorNotes.escaping: what escapes gets out and away, so the energy letter leaves the word

blocks.note: a teaser is a puzzling problem
E = energy in physics; removed

annotation.surface: A stun gun that keeps leaking its charge.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s is 'is': Electric weapon is problem-with-energy-escaping. The first of the two Es is the one that goes.
annotation.definitionFit: A trade name used generically: the Taser is a stun gun firing electrified darts.

entries.clue: Look embarrassed with worry on returning (6)

indicatorNotes.on: one thing on another follows it, so the worry word comes after the colour
indicatorNotes.returning: going back the way it came, so the joined string runs backwards

blocks.note: red in the face
to nag at someone is to worry them

annotation.surface: Someone shyly checking whether their blush is noticed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Look' begins the clue as a verb in the surface; the answer is the noun, from the informal British 'take a gander'.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal British: 'have a gander' means have a look, so the noun stands for look.

entries.clue: Pretentious Lib Dems possibly missing out on power (4)

indicatorNotes.missing out on: to miss out on something is to go without it, so the power letter is absent

blocks.note: the Liberal Democrats are one example of a political party
P = power in physics; removed

annotation.surface: A jibe at a British party for being pretentious and never getting power.
annotation.walkthrough: The Liberal Democrats are a British political party that has rarely held power, which makes the surface a political dig.
annotation.definitionFit: Arty describes affected artistic taste, the pretension of someone showing off their culture.

entries.clue: Unenthusiastic comment on fourth letter in italics? (11)

blocks.note: D is the fourth letter of the alphabet
the comment is the statement that D 'is' something
italic type slopes: it is inclined

annotation.surface: A typesetter remarking on a letter set in italic.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is a remark about a letter: 'D is inclined', since italic type leans. 'Fourth letter' wants to mean the fourth letter of a word; it is the alphabet's.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone disinclined to help is reluctant, unenthusiastic about it.

entries.clue: Airstrip accepting a flight (7)

indicatorNotes.accepting: to accept something is to take it in, so the airstrip takes A inside it

blocks.note: a runway is an airstrip
used as it stands

annotation.surface: An airport taking in one more plane.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flight' is placed to mean an aeroplane journey beside 'Airstrip'; the definition is the other sense, fleeing.
annotation.definitionFit: Flight in the sense of escape: as a noun, a runaway can mean the act of running away, a flight from danger.

entries.clue: Musical Dylan Thomas uncovered, good for its year (8)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: with its covers taken off, each name loses its first and last letters
indicatorNotes.for: in the sense 'in exchange for', OK stands in place of the year letter

blocks.note: DYLAN without its outer letters
THOMAS without its outer letters
OK = good, put in place of Y (year)

annotation.surface: A claim to have found a musical by the Welsh poet Dylan Thomas.
annotation.walkthrough: Stripping both names gives YLAHOMA; then the Y (year) is swapped for OK. Dylan Thomas was a Welsh poet, never a composer of musicals.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Oklahoma! is one musical, the 1943 Rodgers and Hammerstein show.

entries.clue: Hurry and start cooking seafood (3,4,6,2)

blocks.note: a British idiom for moving faster
skate is a flatfish; putting it on the stove starts the cooking

annotation.surface: Instructions from a busy kitchen to get the fish going quickly.
annotation.walkthrough: The idiom is read literally: skate is a flatfish, and to get it 'on' is to put it on the heat. 'Get your skates on' is British for hurry up.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses: a British idiom for hurrying up, and read literally, putting your skate (the fish) on the heat.

entries.clue: One studying words of Mass dedicated to the Virgin (10)

blocks.note: a gram is a unit of mass
Marian = devoted to the Virgin Mary

annotation.surface: A scholar of the Latin Mass devoted to the Virgin Mary.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital M makes 'Mass' the church service; it is the physical quantity. 'Words of Mass' looks like one phrase but splits after 'words'.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: a grammarian studies how words behave and combine, the rules of a language.

entries.clue: Modification of lasses’ genes producing eternal youth (11)

indicatorNotes.Modification of: to modify something is to change it, here changing the order of the letters

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: Genetic engineering on young women to keep them forever young.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is already about gene editing and youth, so the anagram and the definition sit comfortably in the same scene.
annotation.definitionFit: Near-synonym: never ageing and staying young forever describe the same state.

entries.clue: Be very sure political obsessive’s coming back (4)

indicatorNotes.coming back: something coming back travels the opposite way, so the word runs backwards

blocks.note: a policy wonk is obsessed with political detail; ’s = is

annotation.surface: A confident politics nerd making a comeback.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s is 'is', joining the obsessive to the instruction. Wonk is informal for someone obsessed with policy detail.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb for verb: to be certain of a fact is to have knowledge of it, not merely believe it.

entries.clue: Planned to return to prison, perhaps? (10)

blocks.note: done on purpose, not by accident
the reverse of setting someone free: a jokey coinage

annotation.surface: A reoffender who meant to be locked up again.
annotation.walkthrough: The second sense is invented: DE- undoes things, so to de-liberate someone reverses their liberation. The question mark flags the made-up word.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: an adjective meaning intentional, and a whimsical verb 'de-liberate', to undo a release.

entries.clue: Note returning ship’s officer put uniform on? (5,2)

indicatorNotes.returning: going back the way it came, so the officer's title runs backwards

blocks.note: D is a musical note
pusser is Royal Navy slang for the purser, the officer in charge of stores

annotation.surface: A sailor coming home and changing into uniform.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ship's officer' invites PURSER, which is one letter wrong; the naval slang form is the one that fits.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: putting a uniform on is one way to dress up, and the question mark admits it.

entries.clue: Schoolmarm possibly introducing rubbish project (8)

indicatorNotes.introducing: to introduce is to bring in, so the rubbish is brought inside the prude

blocks.note: a prim schoolmarm is one example of a prude
rot = nonsense, rubbish

annotation.surface: A strict teacher bringing in a worthless school project.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Project' sits like a school assignment; it is the verb, stressed on the second syllable.
annotation.definitionFit: Verb for verb: a ledge that projects from a wall sticks out from it.

entries.clue: Covering past song (7)

blocks.note: over = past, finished
a lay is an old word for a song or ballad

annotation.surface: A cover version of an old song.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a musician 'covering' a past song; the definition is a literal covering.
annotation.definitionFit: Noun for noun: a layer spread over a surface, such as gold leaf, is a covering.

entries.clue: Now here’s one that has it at whichever point in history? (7)

indicatorNotes.that has it: a phrase that has the answer holds it inside, so the letters are there to find

blocks.note: noW HERE'S One

annotation.surface: A presenter offering an example that dates from some unknown time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In history' marks the definition as archaic. The question mark admits that 'point' means a place, not a moment.
annotation.definitionFit: An archaic word: whereso meant wheresoever, at whatever point or place.

entries.clue: Newt lad disturbed here? (7)

indicatorNotes.disturbed: things disturbed are moved out of place, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A boy startling a newt in a marsh.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and picture: a boy poking about after newts would do it in exactly this sort of place.
annotation.definitionFit: The &lit works because newts breed in ponds and marshes, so the clue describes where the scene happens.

entries.clue: Like cockpit display, audiovisual one with moving icon (7)

indicatorNotes.moving: letters that move change position, so the icon's letters shift about

blocks.note: AV = audiovisual
I = one, the Roman numeral
ICON rearranged

annotation.surface: A description of a cockpit screen with an animated symbol on it.
annotation.walkthrough: The icon on a screen belongs in the cockpit picture, which hides that it is only four letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjective for aircraft electronics: the cockpit's instruments and screens are avionics.

entries.clue: Invention of piano replacing clavier ultimately in performance (7)

indicatorNotes.replacing: one thing replacing another takes its place, so P goes where R stood
indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of clavier is taken
indicatorNotes.in: the swap happens inside the word for a performance

blocks.note: p = piano, quiet in musical notation
the last letter of clavier, taken out
a concert is a performance

annotation.surface: The story of how the piano came to replace the clavier in concerts.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is music history, and every word fits it; P for piano is the musical dynamic marking, not the instrument.
annotation.definitionFit: Invention as a product of the mind: a concept is an idea someone has devised.

entries.clue: King brooded over duty (4)

indicatorNotes.over: turned over, as a page or card is flipped, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: K = king, in chess
a hen sat on, or brooded, her eggs

annotation.surface: A king moping about his obligations.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Brooded over' looks like sulking about the duty; 'brooded' is a hen sitting on eggs, and 'over' is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a duty assigned to you is a task.

entries.clue: Great struggle with department put years on academic (10)

blocks.note: an arm is a branch or department of an organisation
aged = made older
a don is a university teacher, especially at Oxford or Cambridge

annotation.surface: A university's bitter fight to make a lecturer work for years longer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Put years on academic' reads as one action done to a person; it splits in two.
annotation.definitionFit: From the Book of Revelation: the site of the last battle, now any huge catastrophic conflict.

entries.clue: Alert and with a keen eye for starters (5)

indicatorNotes.for starters: starters are what comes first, so each word gives its first letter

blocks.note: first letters of And With A Keen Eye

annotation.surface: A description of someone watchful and sharp-eyed.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay words are themselves a description of an alert person, so the whole clue reads as one character sketch.
annotation.definitionFit: Adjective for adjective: alert to a danger and awake to it mean the same, being conscious of it.

entries.clue: Pleasing foxtrot tune (4)

blocks.note: Foxtrot is F in the NATO phonetic alphabet
an air is a tune

annotation.surface: Praise for a nice dance tune.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Foxtrot tune' reads as music for the dance; foxtrot is the radio code word for its initial.
annotation.definitionFit: A slightly literary sense: pleasing to the eye, as in 'fair maiden'.

entries.clue: Queen set down outside a pioneering TV location (9,6)

indicatorNotes.outside: one thing outside another surrounds it, so the setting-down word wraps round A

blocks.note: Queen Alexandra, wife of Edward VII
to place something is to set it down
used as it stands

annotation.surface: A monarch putting something down beside a famous broadcasting site.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Queen' tempts the solver toward ER or R; here it is a whole royal name. The answer is a Victorian entertainment venue in north London.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: the BBC's first regular public television broadcasts went out from Alexandra Palace in 1936.

entries.clue: Fuss after radioactive gas is released from container (3)

indicatorNotes.is released from container: what is released gets out of its casing, so the gas's inner letters come free of their outer shell

blocks.note: radon is a radioactive gas
RADON without its outer letters R and N

annotation.surface: Panic after radioactive gas leaks from a canister.
annotation.walkthrough: The container is the gas word's own outer shell, R…N, which also happens to be radon's chemical symbol Rn.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, familiar from 'Much Ado About Nothing': a to-do or commotion.

entries.clue: Leave desolate (6)

blocks.note: abandon, walk out on
barren and empty, used as an adjective

annotation.surface: An instruction to abandon someone utterly alone.
annotation.walkthrough: The two senses share a spelling but not a sound: de-ZERT (leave) and DEZ-ert (barren), the second used as an adjective, as in 'a desert island'.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: a verb for abandoning a post or person, and an adjective for an empty, uninhabited place.

entries.clue: Recurrent theme allowed to return as they do in Star Trek? (8)

annotation.definition: as they do in Star Trek?

indicatorNotes.to return: to return is to go back, so the joined pieces run backwards

blocks.note: a trope is a recurring motif
let = allowed

annotation.surface: A familiar science-fiction theme cleared to come back.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: Star Trek crews are famously 'beamed up' between ship and planet.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the transporter in Star Trek moves people instantly, which is what to teleport means.
